title: Hooks
description: Run your own scripts at key moments: format after edits, block dangerous commands.

theory.title: Deterministic reflexes
theory.body:
**Hooks** are shell commands Claude Code runs at specific points in its lifecycle. Unlike an instruction in `CLAUDE.md`, a hook **always** runs; it doesn't rely on Claude remembering.

Key events, in the order they usually happen:
• `SessionStart`: a session begins or resumes
• `UserPromptSubmit`: you send a prompt
• `PreToolUse`: before a tool runs (can block it)
• `PostToolUse`: after a tool call succeeds
• `Notification`: Claude needs input or permission
• `Stop`: Claude finishes responding
Also: `SubagentStop`, `PreCompact`, `SessionEnd`.

theory.title: Anatomy of a hook config
theory.body:
Hooks live under `"hooks"` in a settings file such as `.claude/settings.json`. Read it from the outside in:
1. **Event** (`"PostToolUse"`): when to run. Holds a list `[ ]` of matcher groups.
2. **`"matcher"`**: which tools trigger it, by tool name. `"Edit|Write"` means Edit **or** Write; `"Bash"` means shell commands; `"*"` or empty matches every tool.
3. **`"hooks"`**: a list of handlers to run.
4. **Handler**: `"type": "command"` means "run a shell command", and `"command"` is that command.

This one formats every file Claude edits or writes with Prettier.

theory.title: What the hook receives
theory.body:
Claude Code sends your command a JSON description of the event on **stdin** (the input piped into it), with fields like `tool_name` and `tool_input`. For Edit and Write, `tool_input.file_path` is the file that changed.

In the Prettier hook, `jq -r '.tool_input.file_path'` pulls out that path, and `| xargs npx prettier --write` passes it to Prettier.

Inside a session, type `/hooks` to browse the hooks you have configured.

exercises.prompt: Match each hook event to when it fires.
exercises.explanation: Each event is a different moment in the lifecycle, so picking the right one decides whether your script can block, react or report.

exercises.prompt: Why use a hook instead of "always run prettier" in CLAUDE.md?
options: Hooks make Claude use fewer tokens
A hook runs every time, deterministically; an instruction depends on Claude remembering
exercises.explanation: A hook is run by Claude Code itself every time, whereas an instruction depends on the model remembering it.

exercises.prompt: How does a command hook find out which file Claude just edited?
options: It reads JSON from stdin, e.g. tool_input.file_path
exercises.explanation: Claude Code pipes the event details as JSON into stdin, so tools like `jq` can pull out fields such as `tool_input.file_path`.

exercises.prompt: Which matcher value matches every tool?
exercises.explanation: A `"*"` matcher (or an empty one) applies the hook to every tool, so use a specific name when you only want some tools.

exercises.prompt: You want consistent formatting after every edit. Which request to Claude is better?
options: Please remember to format files from now on.
Add a PostToolUse hook to .claude/settings.json with matcher Edit|Write that pipes tool_input.file_path to npx prettier --write.
exercises.explanation: A hook makes formatting happen automatically every time, whereas a reminder is only a request the model may forget.

exercises.prompt: Run Prettier on every file Claude edits or writes.
exercises.explanation: PostToolUse runs after the file is written, `Edit|Write` limits it to file-changing tools, and `"command"` tells Claude Code to run a shell command.

exercises.prompt: An edit happens. Put the hook moments in order.
steps: PreToolUse hooks run before the Edit
The Edit tool changes the file
exercises.explanation: Pre hooks run before a tool so they can block it, Post hooks run after it succeeds, and Stop fires when the reply ends.

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, type the slash command that shows your configured hooks.
exercises.hint: Pattern: / + the name of the feature.
exercises.explanation: `/hooks` lists the hooks from all your settings files, so you can confirm a new hook was registered.

theory.title: Exit codes are the verdict
theory.body:
A `PreToolUse` hook can **block** a tool call. When the script ends:
• `exit 0` = success, the call proceeds.
• `exit 2` = **block** it, and whatever the script printed to **stderr** (`>&2`) is shown to Claude as the reason.

Line by line: read the Bash command from stdin with `jq` (for the Bash tool it is in `tool_input.command`), check it with `grep`, and if it is scary, explain on stderr and exit 2.
theory.code:
#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh
CMD=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command')     # the command Claude wants to run
if echo "$CMD" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then  # does it contain rm -rf?
  echo "Blocked: rm -rf is not allowed" >&2  # reason, on stderr
  exit 2                                    # block!
fi
exit 0                                      # anything else: allow

theory.title: Make it executable
theory.body: Claude Code can only run a script file that has the **executable** permission. Set it once with `chmod +x` followed by the script path (`chmod u+x` or `chmod 755` also work).

theory.title: Wiring it up
theory.body:
Register the script under `PreToolUse` (before the tool runs, so it can still block) with matcher `"Bash"` (only shell commands). Same shape as last lesson: event → matcher → hooks → command.

`$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is a variable holding the project root path, so the script is found from any subfolder. The `\"` marks are quotes escaped inside a JSON string; they wrap the path in case it contains spaces.

Hooks can live in `~/.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`. A hook cannot override a **deny** rule: even if the hook says allow, deny still wins.

exercises.prompt: Which exit code from a PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call?
exercises.explanation: Claude Code treats exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook as "block", while 0 lets the call proceed.

exercises.prompt: When a PreToolUse hook exits with 2, where does its explanation go?
options: Its stderr is shown to Claude as the reason
exercises.explanation: The stderr text is handed to Claude as the reason, so it can understand the block and try a safer approach.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece to its meaning.
exercises.explanation: Exit codes and stderr are the only way a command hook talks back to Claude Code, so each one carries a specific meaning.

exercises.prompt: A deny rule blocks `Bash(rm *)`, but your PreToolUse hook returns "allow". What happens to `rm temp.txt`?
options: It is still blocked by the deny rule
The hook wins, so it runs
exercises.explanation: Deny rules are enforced regardless of what a hook returns, so a hook can add blocks but never lift one.

exercises.prompt: Finish the guard script: read the Bash command from stdin and block it.
exercises.code:
CMD=$(jq -r '.tool_input.___')
if echo "$CMD" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  echo "Blocked: rm -rf is not allowed" >&2
  exit ___
fi
exit 0
exercises.explanation: The Bash tool puts its command in `tool_input.command`, and exiting with 2 is the signal Claude Code reads as "block this call".
exercises.hint: For the Bash tool the command is in tool_input.command; exit 2 blocks, exit 0 allows.

exercises.prompt: Register the guard so it runs before every Bash command.
exercises.explanation: Only a PreToolUse hook runs early enough to block, `Bash` limits it to shell commands, and `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` makes the script path work from any folder.
exercises.hint: Blocking needs the "before" event; the matcher is the tool name; the project root variable is CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.

exercises.prompt: Set up a guardrail hook from scratch.
steps: Add a PreToolUse entry with matcher Bash in .claude/settings.json
Run /hooks to confirm it is registered
Ask Claude to rm -rf a temp folder and watch it get blocked
exercises.explanation: A hook only works once it exists, is executable and is registered, and testing it proves the block really fires.

exercises.prompt: Make your hook script `.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh` executable using `chmod`.
exercises.explanation: Claude Code can only run a script that has the executable permission, which `chmod +x` adds.

exercises.scenario: Ask Claude to create a hook that stops it from ever editing .env files or package-lock.json.
exercises.sample: Claude has accidentally edited our secrets and lockfile before, so I want a hard guard. Create .claude/hooks/protect-files.sh that reads the hook JSON from stdin, extracts tool_input.file_path with jq, and exits 2 with a clear stderr message if the path matches .env, .env.* or package-lock.json. Make it executable and register it in @.claude/settings.json as a PreToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write using "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR". Constraint: don't modify any other hooks already in the file. Done when /hooks lists it and you show me the final config.
exercises.explanation: A precise hook request names the reason, event, matcher, protected paths, blocking mechanism and how to verify it.

mission.title: Hook Master
mission.intro: Give Kip some reflexes: auto-format after edits and refuse dangerous commands.
checklist: Add a PostToolUse hook with matcher `Edit|Write` that runs Prettier to `.claude/settings.json`
Ask Claude to edit a JS file and confirm it comes out formatted
Write `.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh` that exits 2 on `rm -rf`, `chmod +x` it, and register it under PreToolUse with matcher `Bash`
Run `/hooks` and confirm both hooks are listed
Ask Claude to `rm -rf` a temp folder and watch the hook block it
mission.explanation: Hooks turn your team rules into guarantees that run every single time.

cheatsheet.description: Runs before a tool call; exit 2 blocks it.

Fires when Claude needs your input or permission.
Fires when a session begins or resumes.
Filters by tool name, e.g. "Bash" or "Edit|Write".
